incidents.title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
incidents.summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with more than 30 years of experience, has discovered that criminals are using artificial intelligence to impersonate him and defraud vulnerable immigrants. Scammers created hundreds of fake videos and social media profiles featuring AI-generated images of Leal offering immigration services he never provides. In one video, a digital version of Leal promises US residency assistance to undocumented immigrants for $2,200. Leal first learned of the scheme when potential clients began calling his office, though suspicious activity began last October and dramatically escalated over the past three months.

Leal's office hired an anti-piracy company that has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles across social media platforms, including 3,500 on TikTok, 2,400 on Facebook, and 544 on Instagram. The scams typically start with social media videos directing people to contact a WhatsApp number, where fraudsters send fake contracts and collect payment through apps like Venmo, Zelle, and Cash App. Leal has changed his personal phone number and plans to contact local and federal authorities to investigate. He warns immigrants to verify the identity of anyone offering legal services online and to be cautious of social media advertisements requesting immediate payment.

incidents.title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
incidents.summary:
A fake online article featured a fabricated interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock discussing Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The article depicted an increasingly heated exchange where Bullock supposedly stormed out over Kohler's questions about the platform's alleged market exploitation algorithm. However, this interview never actually occurred. The scam represents a growing trend of AI-generated investment fraud that Australian financial regulators say is becoming more prevalent and sophisticated.

The corporate watchdog ASIC released research showing a significant rise in these deceptive schemes, removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. Phishing scams jumped 279 percent, while fake investment platforms increased by 151 percent. Kohler ranks among the most commonly impersonated Australians, alongside Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, politicians like Pauline Hanson and Angus Taylor, and wealthy individuals including Gina Rinehart and Dick Smith. ASIC warns consumers to verify financial services licenses through its public registers and avoid websites lacking verifiable credentials. The regulator advises that polished content and familiar branding do not guarantee legitimacy.

incidents.title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork
incidents.summary:
A lawsuit has been filed against Oura, the smart ring manufacturer, accusing the company of false advertising regarding its sleep tracking capabilities. The Clarkson Law Firm filed the proposed class-action suit in San Francisco on Thursday, claiming that Oura's rings, which cost $300 and up, cannot accurately measure sleep stages despite marketing claims stating they have 95% accuracy compared to clinical sleep labs. The lawsuit argues that Oura's sensors and algorithms rely on unreliable AI-generated estimates rather than actual physiological measurements needed for precise sleep stage detection.

Oura responded by defending its products, stating it stands behind its research and accuracy claims. The company explained that its rings estimate sleep stages using multiple physiological signals including heart rate, breathing patterns, and temperature, and that independent studies have validated these measurements against the gold standard polysomnography test. The lawsuit seeks class-action status and a jury trial, though it remains unclear what compensation customers could receive. This is not Oura's first legal challenge, as the company faces another ongoing class-action suit alleging it collected personal data without customer consent.

incidents.title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations
incidents.summary:
Minnesota attorney Faisal S. Ahmed faced disciplinary action after submitting fabricated court cases to a judge in a civil lawsuit. Ahmed cited two nonexistent cases, Anderson v. City of Biwabik and Doherty v. Alma E. Clark Memorial Home, in a legal memorandum filed in Hennepin County Court. The opposing attorney discovered the fake citations were generated by artificial intelligence tools. The judge ultimately ruled against Ahmed's client and ordered payment of $233,563 in back rent to a property owner suing a Robbinsdale food store owner for unpaid rent.

Ahmed agreed to a 30-day suspension of his law license and must pay $5,000 in fines plus $900 in costs. Judge Lois Conroy highlighted that while AI can assist attorneys, it should not replace legal analysis or be used blindly. The case reflects a broader problem, with over 800 documented instances of litigants using AI to create fake legal citations. Minnesota's Office of Lawyers Professional Responsibility noted this conduct caused unnecessary delays and burdened the court and opposing counsel.

incidents.title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that the Aurora ransomware group, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi environments and is exploiting virtual machine infrastructure. The group operates a data leak site and has victimized organizations across multiple countries. Between April 8 and May 21, 2026, Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation attacks against ten target organizations. The attackers tasked the AI agent with various activities including installing VPN clients, scanning internal networks, enumerating domain privileges, and attempting credential theft attacks, while explicitly restricting certain high-risk techniques like DCSync attacks and account lockouts.

The discovered Aurora ransomware encrypts files using ChaCha20 encryption and includes special functionality to target virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can view ransom demands. A custom tool called esxi_finder.py scans victim networks to identify ESXi hosts and vCenter servers. Researchers also identified a second Aurora cluster involving eight victims across six countries that used different techniques, including SQL Server exploitation and S3 bucket exfiltration. The investigation provides multiple indicators of compromise including IP addresses, domains, and file hashes for security teams to track the group's ongoing operations.

incidents.title: A Pizza Hut franchisee is suing over a forced AI system it says wrecked deliveries
incidents.summary:
A major Pizza Hut franchisee filed a lawsuit in May alleging that the chain's AI-powered delivery system, called Dragontail, caused over $100 million in damages. Chaac Pizza Northeast, which operates approximately 111 Pizza Hut locations across the Northeast, claims the system created operational problems and customer dissatisfaction after Pizza Hut mandated its adoption in 2024. The software gave DoorDash drivers real-time visibility into kitchen workflows, causing drivers to wait up to fifteen minutes to batch multiple orders together rather than delivering pizzas immediately, which slowed deliveries and led to cold arrivals.

Before the rollout, Chaac achieved over 90% on-time delivery within thirty minutes and maintained double-digit sales growth. After implementing Dragontail, the franchisee experienced sharp performance declines, with New York City sales dropping from positive 10.19% to negative 9.78% year-over-year. The lawsuit argues Pizza Hut breached its franchise agreement by forcing continued use of the problematic software without adequate training, support, or system modifications. Pizza Hut stated it would respond through legal channels but declined further comment.

incidents.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
incidents.summary:
Scammers are sending personalized emails impersonating Terry Gross and other staff members of NPR's "Fresh Air" program to solicit money from potential interview guests. Authors, entertainers and public figures have received highly detailed messages that reference their work and propose interview topics, making the invitations appear legitimate. The scam typically escalates when victims are asked to pay fees for production costs, with some emails even requesting social media login credentials. WHYY, NPR and Fresh Air have confirmed they are aware of these fraudulent emails and are investigating with law enforcement.

Cybersecurity experts explain that artificial intelligence has made impersonation scams more convincing and personalized than traditional fraud attempts. Red flags include requests for payment, emails from suspicious addresses like terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com, and the implausibility of a major show's host personally handling booking logistics. WHYY has emphasized it never charges guests for interviews and recommends victims verify suspicious requests by calling the organization directly through official channels rather than responding to suspicious emails.

incidents.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
incidents.summary:
# Summary

An Israeli-funded fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days using a platform designed to optimize content for artificial intelligence chatbots. The nonexistent institute, which has no legal entity, physical address, or named staff, presented pro-Israel positions on topics including Palestinian prisoner torture, war crimes allegations, and Gaza starvation as neutral academic research. The New York media company Piro Inc filed the site with the US Justice Department as material distributed for the Israeli government under foreign agent registration law.

The operation is part of a broader effort costing tens of millions of dollars financed by Israel through intermediaries including European advertising group Havas Media. The campaign aims to influence chatbot responses and training data so they cite pro-Israel arguments. Israeli officials have expressed doubts about the public diplomacy campaign's effectiveness, with one calling it a failure despite large spending. Recent polling shows American support for Israel has declined significantly, with only 36 percent sympathizing with Israel and 60 percent viewing it unfavorably as of April 2026.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

incidents.title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.
incidents.summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Atlantic Records, and Capitol Records have sued two popular AI music generators, Udio and Suno, for copyright infringement. The labels claim both companies scraped thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models and are now generating music that directly reproduces sections of famous recordings. The lawsuits allege the companies have been deliberately secretive about their training data, though both previously claimed their use of copyrighted material constitutes fair use. The record labels submitted a massive list of scraped works, including music from The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Bruce Springsteen, Michael Jackson, and many others.

To prove their case, the record labels demonstrated they could repeatedly recreate famous songs by using specific prompts describing musical characteristics like decade, genre, and artist style. Examples include generating songs that replicate Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode," Bill Haley's style, and an almost identical version of Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The labels claim this degree of similarity would be impossible if the AI models weren't trained on these copyrighted recordings. The lawsuits were filed in New York and Massachusetts and include unnamed individuals accused of helping scrape the music.

incidents.summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, reaching licensing agreements to end disputes over copyright infringement. UMG had accused Udio of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system, claiming the company created music similar to existing hits like The Temptations' "My Girl" without permission or compensation. Under the settlement, Udio will launch a new platform next year trained only on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, and share songs while compensating artists.

This represents Udio's first major licensing deal with a major music label and marks a shift toward cooperation between the AI industry and music companies. Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, has attracted millions of users since its launch. The company declined to disclose financial terms of the settlement. Additionally, UMG announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers, signaling growing acceptance of AI technology within the music industry.

incidents.title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings
incidents.summary:
State Farm's defense lawyers apologized for using artificial intelligence tools that generated fake legal cases, false quotes, and nonexistent legal holdings in court filings for a lawsuit in Los Angeles. The homeowner, Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, sued State Farm after a 2020 fire in her Carson home made it uninhabitable. While repairs were underway, storm damage occurred, and after delays in getting State Farm's approval, the work was never completed. Meni-Siliga and her husband exhausted their savings, declared bankruptcy, and lost their home to foreclosure. The case is scheduled for trial in October.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted using an AI tool called Irys to help prepare motions, mistakenly believing it performed citation checks. She confirmed seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and fabricated quotes. Lead counsel Kenneth Katel accepted responsibility for the filings. The incident highlights growing concerns about AI use in law firms, with 41% of law firms and 47% of corporate legal departments now using generative AI. A database tracking legal hallucinations worldwide has documented 1,922 cases, mostly in the United States.

stories.Headline: Nvidia buying artificial intelligence platform Hugging Face for $13 billion
stories.Summary:
Chipmaker Nvidia is acquiring Hugging Face, an artificial intelligence software platform, for approximately $13 billion. Hugging Face is used by over 18 million developers, researchers, and creators who share more than 3 million models, 500,000 datasets, and 1 million applications on the platform. More than 200,000 companies also use the service. Nvidia's CEO stated that Hugging Face will remain an open-source platform, allowing organizations to download and customize their own AI models rather than paying for proprietary services from competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic.

The acquisition represents Nvidia's strategic bet that businesses will increasingly favor open-source AI models. This deal comes amid growing concerns about AI security, following several incidents where AI systems hacked into other organizations during testing. The $12.93 billion purchase includes $1 billion for employee retention. Nvidia's stock rose nearly 2% following the announcement, while Hugging Face remains privately held.

stories.Headline: Nevada lawmakers propose oversight for state, local agencies using AI - Kiowa County Press
stories.Summary:
# Summary

Nevada lawmakers are proposing legislation to establish oversight standards for how state and local government agencies use artificial intelligence technology. The bill draft request was approved in August by the interim Government Affairs Committee, with Democratic state Senator Dina Neal championing the proposal. The legislation would require transparency around AI systems and prevent bias in automated decision-making. Several Nevada agencies, including the Department of Employment, Training, and Rehabilitation and the Department of Motor Vehicles, have already implemented AI systems without statutory oversight. Concerns have been raised about cases where people were denied unemployment benefits and could not speak to a human during appeals, highlighting the need for human decision-making in critical processes.

The bill will be considered during the 2027 Legislative Session beginning February 1. Lawmakers anticipate significant pushback from state and local agencies when the proposal comes up for discussion. This effort reflects a broader national trend, as 38 states adopted AI-related policies in 2025. Nevada's push for AI regulation comes despite President Trump's efforts to limit state-level AI regulation through executive orders, though legal experts argue such orders may not prevent state action under constitutional protections for state authority.

stories.Headline: NYC, the nation's largest school district, bans AI for students through 8th grade - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
stories.Summary:
New York City's public school system announced a temporary one-year ban on artificial intelligence tools for students through eighth grade, which Mayor Zohran Mamdani described as the most expansive prohibition in the country. The policy prohibits all software using student-facing generative AI and bans companion chatbots across all grades. Meanwhile, the city will recommend screen time limits of 30 minutes daily for third through fifth graders and 45 minutes for sixth through eighth graders. Teachers remain allowed to use AI for instructional planning and operational tasks.

The broader approach aims to help students navigate AI while preventing over-reliance and cheating. High school students will receive AI literacy classes twice yearly and participate in supervised AI platform pilots. City officials will also conduct a comprehensive review of all technology tools in the school system and eliminate those deemed non-essential to learning. The teachers union praised the screen time limits but expressed concerns about implementation details and called for stronger safeguards in products the district purchases. Students are scheduled to return to classrooms the following week.

stories.Summary:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is proposing a ban on artificial intelligence tools for students in public schools through eighth grade. The policy aims to restrict how AI technology is used in younger classrooms as part of what the mayor describes as creating the right future for children. The Mamdani administration wants schools to carefully control the role that artificial intelligence plays in education.

However, the proposal is facing skepticism from people within New York City's education system. Critics question whether such a broad restriction can actually be enforced, especially as AI tools become increasingly integrated into computers, phones, and common online services. This move places the nation's largest public school system at the center of the growing national debate about how schools should respond to generative artificial intelligence.

stories.Headline: LAUSD adopts moratorium on student AI use, another big move to limit classroom computer time - Los Angeles Times
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles Unified School District has implemented a moratorium on student use of generative artificial intelligence on school devices for the current school year. District administrators enacted the policy independently to align with the school board's June decision to reduce student screen time, though some board members expressed surprise at not being formally notified. The moratorium prohibits chatbots and AI tutors for all students, though the district will continue using non-generative AI tools like adaptive learning systems and speech recognition software. Students can still use Google for searches but cannot access Google's interactive AI Mode on school devices.

The announcement comes as New York City also moved to restrict student AI use, banning generative AI in preschool through eighth grade while allowing limited use in high schools. Activist parents and education organizations praised Los Angeles's stricter approach as a historic step addressing concerns about technology reliance in schools. However, the district has not yet developed policies for student AI use on personal devices, and teachers remain able to use AI tools. Officials are working to determine long-term AI guidelines, as the moratorium currently applies only to the current school year.

Broadcom reported that its AI semiconductor revenue surged 221% to $16.7 billion in its latest fiscal quarter, with overall revenue climbing 86% and earnings per share rising 96%. The company designs custom AI chips for major clients including Anthropic, OpenAI, Alphabet, and Meta Platforms. Management expects fourth quarter revenue of approximately $34.8 billion, slightly below analyst expectations of $35 billion. The article suggests the market overreacted negatively to the earnings report, creating a buying opportunity. Broadcom currently trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 19 times next year's expected earnings, considered reasonable given the anticipated growth from its custom chip business. Analysts believe if the company meets its projected 2027 earnings estimates, the stock could appreciate over 50% if it returns to a typical valuation multiple of 30 times earnings.
